summary: Defines common requirements for Carrier-Grade NATs, which are large NATs run by internet providers to share addresses among many customers. It updates RFC 4787. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: A Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) lets many subscribers share public IPv4 addresses through equipment in an ISP's network. RFC 6888 sets common behavior requirements intended to make that sharing more predictable and fair.

subtitle: Shared requirements for ISP-run IPv4 NATs that serve many subscribers.

tldr.problem: An ISP may use one Carrier-Grade NAT to share public IPv4 addresses among subscribers. Unclear behavior can break applications and let one subscriber consume shared resources unfairly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds requirements for address pooling, resource limits, port reuse, subscriber control, errors, logging, and port allocation on top of existing NAT behavior documents.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 4787. The RFC calls these requirements a minimum interoperability set, not an endorsement of CGNs.

today: RFC 6888 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 127, published in April 2013. It updates RFC 4787, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why CGNs Need Shared Requirements
sections.content:
A CGN is a network address translator in an Internet Service Provider's network that shares an IPv4 address among subscribers. A subscriber may also use a NAT at home, creating two translation layers.

This document defines additional behavior requirements on top of the general NAT requirements for UDP, TCP, and ICMP. It is not an IETF endorsement or a complete CGN specification; its stated purpose is to improve the chance that applications work across CGNs.
sections.plainLanguage: A CGN is a shared translator operated by an ISP rather than by one subscriber. The RFC sets a minimum set of rules for how that translator behaves.

sections.title: Scope of a Carrier-Grade NAT
sections.content:
In this RFC, a CGN is an IPv4-only NAT function that shares an address among several subscribers and is not managed by those subscribers. The term describes where the function is located, not its quality.

The document also applies to the CGN function in Dual-Stack Lite, even though that deployment uses IPv6 to carry traffic to the translator. IPv6 address translation itself is outside this RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The term CGN means a shared IPv4 translator in the ISP network. It does not describe the equipment's quality, and subscriber control is limited or absent.

sections.title: Sharing Addresses and Resources
sections.content:
The default IP address pooling behavior MUST be Paired: sessions from one internal address use the same external address across transport protocols. Administrators MAY change the behavior for an application protocol. A CGN MUST accept contiguous and non-contiguous external address ranges.

A CGN MUST support administrator-configurable limits on external ports or ICMP identifiers assigned to each subscriber. It SHOULD also support limits on state memory and the rate at which state is allocated. Endpoint-independent filtering is RECOMMENDED because some applications require it.
sections.plainLanguage: The default keeps one subscriber's sessions on the same external address. Administrators can limit how many shared ports and how much state each subscriber uses.

sections.title: Port Reuse, Subscriber Control and Errors
sections.content:
After an external port is released, it SHOULD NOT be assigned to a new mapping for at least 120 seconds. The wait also applies after a CGN loses its state, subject to the exceptions in the RFC. The administrator must be able to configure the wait and the maximum number of ports in this state.

A CGN MUST provide a protocol that lets subscribers control mappings; Port Control Protocol is the recommended choice. If resource limits prevent a new mapping, the CGN MUST drop the new packet and MUST NOT delete existing mappings to make room. It SHOULD send an ICMP Destination Unreachable with code 1 and notify a management system when configured.
sections.plainLanguage: A released port waits before being assigned to a different mapping, which reduces the chance that delayed traffic reaches the wrong session. If resources run out, the CGN rejects new traffic rather than breaking existing mappings.

sections.title: Logging Without Unneeded Destination Data
sections.content:
To identify a subscriber from an abuse report, an administrator may need a transport protocol, subscriber identifier, external source address, external source port, and timestamp. The RFC presents these as useful logging fields, not as a requirement.

A CGN SHOULD NOT log destination addresses or ports unless an administrative reason requires it. The document notes that destination logging creates privacy concerns and can increase the volume of stored logs.
sections.plainLanguage: Mapping records can help an administrator identify which subscriber used an external port at a given time. The CGN should avoid recording destinations unless needed for an administrative reason.

sections.title: Port Allocation Trade-Offs
sections.content:
The port allocation scheme SHOULD aim to use ports efficiently, reduce log volume, and make port numbers difficult for attackers to guess. These goals compete: a scheme that improves one can make another harder to achieve.

The RFC therefore states these as SHOULD-level requirements rather than MUST requirements. Implementers and operators need to choose a scheme that balances the three goals.
sections.plainLanguage: Port allocation has three goals: use ports efficiently, limit logging, and make port numbers difficult to guess. A scheme may improve one goal while making another harder.

sections.title: Security and Subscriber Fairness
sections.content:
A subscriber who spoofs another subscriber's customer-premises equipment could consume that subscriber's allowed mappings and cause denial of service. The RFC points to ingress filtering as a way for an ISP to prevent this.

The recommended default filtering behavior has security considerations described by RFC 4787. The document also notes the security issues that can arise if a NAT reassembles IP fragments.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscriber might try to use another subscriber's identity to consume their mapping allowance. The RFC points to source-address filtering as a defense.

viz.caption: Selected requirements for fair CGN operation

items.label: Paired pooling
items.desc: Must be the default address-pooling behavior.

items.label: Port reuse
items.desc: Should wait at least 120 seconds, subject to listed exceptions.

items.label: Resource limit
items.desc: Must drop new traffic and retain existing mappings.

items.label: Destination logging
items.desc: Should not log destinations without an administrative need.
